findings.title: Export audio mix time grows quadratically with timeline length
findings.suggested_fix: Make the node count O(clips) instead of O(decoded buffers): per audio clip, allocate one AudioBuffer with mixer.createBuffer(channels, Math.ceil((end - start) * sampleRate), sampleRate), copy each decoded buffer into it with copyToChannel at Math.round((timestamp - start) * sampleRate) (clamping the head and tail to the trim range), then create ONE AudioBufferSourceNode and ONE GainNode per clip and start it at clip.start / FPS. This also removes per-buffer scheduling seams. To bound memory as well, render the mix in fixed windows (for example 10 s OfflineAudioContexts) and call audio.add(chunk) per window instead of one startRendering for the whole timeline. Assumption: channel count and sample rate are constant within a track. Verify with an export test on an AAC or Opus source of at least 60 s that asserts time to the first onProgress above 0.1.
findings.first_evidence: src/export.ts:125-129 -- const source = mixer.createBufferSource(); source.buffer = buffer; const gain = mixer.createGain(); gain.gain.value = clip.track === 'music' ? 0.22 : 1; source.connect(gain).connect(mixer.destination);
findings.why_it_matters: Exporting anything longer than the 12-second demo with audio sits at 0% for minutes before the first video frame is encoded, and the wait quadruples each time the timeline doubles. The offline mix creates one AudioBufferSourceNode plus one GainNode for every decoded buffer (about 47 per second per audio clip for AAC, 50 for Opus), and Chromium processes every connected node on every 128-frame render quantum, so cost is nodes x quanta = O(duration^2). Measured in headless Chromium 157 with the same graph shape (2 tracks, 1024-frame buffers, source -> gain -> destination): 15 s of audio rendered in 3.0 s, 30 s in 12.8 s, 60 s in 98 s; the same 60 s with one source node per clip rendered in 0.055 s. Sharing one gain per clip only cut 60 s to 33 s, so the node count itself is the cost. Every decoded buffer also stays referenced by its node until startRendering resolves, so all decoded PCM for all audio clips (about 23 MB per clip-minute at 48 kHz stereo float32) is live at once alongside the 23 MB/minute mix buffer, which is far more than the documented 'export buffers data in memory' implies for audio encoded at 128 kbps.

findings.title: Project save fails past about 400 MB of media
findings.suggested_fix: Two steps; the second removes the ceiling. (1) Short term, in serializeProject before encoding: sum the blob sizes of the assets to be written and throw an actionable error when the base64 total would exceed the string limit (about 380 MB raw), e.g. `Project media totals ${mb} MB; this version can save about 380 MB. Remove unused media or shorten sources.`, and show the same warning from importFiles when the running total crosses it. (2) Structural: never hold all media in one JS string. Encode natively (FileReader.readAsDataURL(blob), or bytes.toBase64() where available) instead of the String.fromCharCode loop plus btoa; split parseProject into an envelope validator (clips, zooms, layout, muted, media ids) and a per-media data validator so serializeProject validates the snapshot without parseProject(JSON.stringify(...)); emit the file as Blob parts, new Blob([head, dataUrl1, sep, dataUrl2, ..., tail]). On open, replace btoa(atob(match[1])) !== match[1] with an O(1) check of the final quantum's unused bits. A version-3 container (JSON manifest followed by raw media parts, read back with file.slice()) lifts the cap on open as well and fits the version bump that per-asset pointer data needs anyway. Decision left to the owner: whether save should embed only assets a clip references (reliability proposed it; it changes what a reopened library contains). Keep the non-canonical base64 cases in src/project.test.ts as the regression gate and add a save/reopen test with realistically sized media. Assumption: Chrome/V8 is the target runtime.

findings.title: Multi-commit push slips baseline growth past shrink-only gate
findings.suggested_fix: Compare against the commit main pointed at before the push: `npm run check:code -- --fail-on-baseline-growth --baseline-base "${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.event.before || 'HEAD^' }}"`, falling back to HEAD^ for workflow_dispatch and for an all-zero `before`. fetch-depth: 0 is already set, so the ref resolves; fallow exits 2 when it cannot, which fails closed. Update the README sentence at README.md:57-59 ("compared with the previous commit") to match. If a pull_request trigger is added (separate finding, #35), pass the PR base SHA there. Assumption: main is not force-pushed; after a force-push `before` may be unreachable and the job fails rather than passes.
findings.why_it_matters: The complexity baseline is advertised as shrink-only, but CI goes green when a new hotspot and its re-saved baseline arrive in any commit other than the last one of a push. The workflow runs only on push to main, checks only the tip, and compares the baseline with HEAD^, so growth introduced one commit earlier is already present at the comparison base. Two commits pushed together, a fast-forwarded branch, or a quick follow-up push (cancel-in-progress kills the earlier run) all pass. Adversarial reproduced it in a throwaway clone: the exact CI command failed on the commit that grew the baseline and exited 0 after one unrelated commit on top.

findings.title: Continuous controls flood the 50-step undo history
findings.suggested_fix: Fix it once in `change` (src/App.tsx:507-513), which every call site goes through. (1) Return early when the next edit is value-equal to the current one; trimClip returns a fresh object, so compare fields or JSON, not identity. (2) Coalesce continuous input: give `change` an optional key (`'layout.radius'`, `zoom:${id}:scale`, `zoom:${id}:focus`) kept in a ref; when the key matches the previous call inside one gesture, replace `edit` without pushing a history entry, and clear the key on any differently-keyed or unkeyed change and in undo(). Decision for the implementer: the gesture boundary. Julik proposed a time window (same key within 800 ms); the stricter alternative is to preview locally and commit on pointerup or blur. Add a Playwright case: split, drag the radius slider with real mouse moves, press Undo twice, expect the split to be undone. Assumption: one undo step per gesture is the intended semantics; the existing tests (tests/refinements.spec.ts:45, :56) only undo single discrete actions and keep passing.
findings.why_it_matters: Dragging the Corner radius slider across its range pushes up to 60 undo steps, one per intermediate value, into a history capped at 50. A single drag therefore wipes out every earlier split, delete, insert and trim from undo, and Ctrl+Z afterwards walks the radius back one pixel per press. The Zoom level slider (up to 20 entries per drag), the crop and zoom number fields, and each arrow press in mouse-marking mode, including key auto-repeat, behave the same way. Actions that change nothing also consume entries: clicking a trim grip without moving it, dragging it outward, or pressing the arrow that would lengthen the clip records an identical state, so the next Undo reports "Undid last edit." and changes nothing. The cause is that every `input` event calls `change()`, which always pushes the previous edit. The pointer-event cursor work and click-generated zooms planned next add more continuous controls on the same path, so the history needs a gesture boundary before then.

findings.title: Export allocates a new full-size canvas per decoded frame
findings.suggested_fix: Pass a pool to the sink: new CanvasSink(track, { poolSize: 2 }).canvasesAtTimestamps(times). The loop at export.ts:176-191 consumes each canvas synchronously before requesting the next one from the same iterator, and mediabunny maps samples to canvases lazily one at a time, so a pool of 2 cannot hand back a canvas that is still in use. Verify with the existing HD and 4K export specs (frame content checks) to confirm no frame is overwritten before it is drawn.
findings.why_it_matters: Every exported frame allocates and discards a source-resolution canvas for each visible video layer (8 MB of pixels at 1080p, 33 MB for a 4K source), so a 10-minute two-layer export churns through 36,000 canvases whose backing stores are only reclaimed when garbage collection gets to them. That slows the render loop and inflates transient memory on top of the documented fully buffered output. mediabunny creates a fresh canvas whenever poolSize is unset and documents the pool as the way to keep allocated VRAM constant; the export draws each sample immediately and never keeps it past the next iterator.next(), so a small ring buffer is safe here. In a throwaway headless Chromium benchmark (software canvas, 1080p), allocate-per-frame cost 7.7 ms per frame against 2.2 ms with one reused canvas.

Pointerdown stores a copy of the clip and selects it; S splits that clip at the playhead (the window shortcut handler is not gated during a drag); pointerup then writes the stored full-length copy, minus the drag, back over the shortened first half, so it overlaps the new second half in both preview and export. Ctrl+Z during the drag has the same shape: the release re-applies the pre-undo clip. Pressing Delete during the drag unmounts the grip, so neither pointerup nor pointercancel runs and `drag` stays set; if the clip is later restored by Undo it renders with the stale trim preview and follows the un-pressed mouse on hover. Resolving the clip by id from current props at commit time removes the snapshot.

report_only.decision_needed: Product/design decision: whether zooms belong to the screen track and ripple with it (and what happens to a zoom spanning the insert point: split, stretch or leave), or whether a zoom is anchored to (assetId, source frame) and derived through the clip list. The second also decides the model click-generated zooms persist.

Design decision: the unit of Zoom.x/y. Source-frame percent (focus keeps pointing at the same recorded pixel when crop changes; version-2 files migrate on open) or mask-space percent (documented on the type; pointer events converted through the cover crop at generation time and stale after a crop edit).

Workflow decision for the repository owner: README.md:53 documents "GitHub CI runs on pushes to `main`" as the current design. Either add a pull_request trigger (and pass the PR base SHA to --baseline-base), or keep main-only CI and state in AGENTS.md that other branches need `gh workflow run ci.yml --ref <branch>`.

residual_risks: Design note for the cursor work (performance, src/timeline.ts:80-81; routed here from a single-reviewer P2 finding): the only per-frame "what applies at this frame" lookup is a linear zooms.find, run twice per frame in zoomCamera and zoomAt. It costs nothing today. The MP4 export branch is the default for branded Chrome and has never run (reliability, src/export.ts:62-64; routed here from a single-reviewer P2 finding on a documented limit): export prefers MP4 whenever the browser can encode AVC (and AAC with audio), CI runs Playwright's bundled Chromium, never sets CHROME_PATH (.github/workflows/ci.yml:42), and tests/export.spec.ts:210 accepts either container, so nothing shows which branch ran. Renaming one module (for example src/Timeline.tsx to src/TimelineView.tsx, re-keying its fallow baseline entries in the same change) removes the ambiguity.

Playhead past the end after a delete, trim or undo shortens the sequence (correctness, testing, julik, adversarial): src/App.tsx has no clamp of its own on frame/frameRef against duration (seek clamps only on the next explicit seek at :524). Julik read the Remotion 4.0.543 sources and found it is not a defect today only because the Player re-dispatches frameupdate when its clamped frame changes; that is a Player internal, not confirmed in a browser. Export draws an empty panel when a decode yields no sample (reliability, src/export.ts:176-178): `if (!sample) continue;` skips the draw, and mediabunny documents that canvasesAtTimestamps may yield null before a track's first timestamp; an iterator that ends early returns undefined. Holding the previous frame and throwing when the iterator ends early would remove the silent case.

Import, Open project and Save have no cancel and no progress (reliability, performance): busy keeps the workspace inert until readMedia has decoded the whole audio track for peaks (src/media.ts:39) or the whole project is re-encoded, so a very long recording locks the editor with only a reload, which discards the edit, as the way out. This follows from the documented full-decode limit; no cheap fix was found short of deferring peaks.

Reverse shuttle and held keys (julik, code-read only): the rewind tick accumulates wall-clock time across a hidden tab (src/App.tsx:580; requestAnimationFrame stops and `last` is not reset, so the first tick after returning rewinds by the whole time away), and holding Space toggles play/pause on every key auto-repeat because event.repeat is not checked (:617).

SourceMonitor reports every play() rejection as a codec failure (julik, src/App.tsx:89-94), including the AbortError raised when Pause is clicked or the asset is switched before play resolves, and a later successful play does not clear the error. downloadBlob revokes the object URL synchronously after anchor.click() on a detached anchor (reliability, julik; src/App.tsx:687-694). The Chromium Playwright downloads prove it there; other WebCodecs browsers were not checked. The success message is shown whether or not the browser wrote the file.

trimClip rounding (testing): the mutant "no Math.round of the delta" survives. parseProject zoom and layout bounds (testing): mutants "zoom range unchecked", "zoom duration 0 accepted", "zoom scale below 1 accepted", "zoom y unbounded" and "layout.screenX unbounded" survive. validateSources track rules (testing): mutants "camera track accepts audio-only media" and "music track accepts media without audio" survive; only the screen and voice arms are tested (src/project.test.ts:217, :224-228).

serializeProject (testing): mutants "no snapshot of edit", "sources not validated before save" and "single spread call (no chunking)" survive. Cancel export from the UI (testing, reliability): the "Cancel export" button and the "Export cancelled." status (src/App.tsx:906, :766-767) are untested; cancellation is exercised only by aborting renderVideo directly. Before the cursor overlay lands, add a fixture with an active zoom and a large pointer sidecar and assert dropped video frames via getVideoPlaybackQuality or requestVideoFrameCallback.

demoted.title: Per-frame linear find pattern will not scale to pointer samples
demoted.why_it_matters: Today this costs nothing: the only per-frame lookup is a scan of a handful of zooms, done twice per frame. It matters because it is the one template in the codebase for 'what applies at this frame', it runs inside the Remotion clock in preview and inside the export frame loop, and the cursor overlay will be written next to it. Applied to the stated 222,749-sample recording, the same find-by-range pattern measured 0.48 ms per frame on average (growing toward the end of the recording), and a filter-style smoothing window measured 2.9 ms per frame; on the performance gate's 4x CPU throttle that is roughly 2 ms to 11 ms of a 33 ms frame, and over a 10-minute export it adds 8.6 s to 51.6 s of pure scanning. A binary search over the same data measured 0.0008 ms per frame. Generated click zooms raise the zoom count too, but hundreds of zooms stay negligible; the sample lookup is what needs an index.
evidence: src/timeline.ts:80-81 -- const zoom = zooms.find((z) => frame >= z.start && frame < z.start + z.duration); const scale = zoomAt(zooms, frame);
src/timeline.ts:54 -- const zoom = zooms.find((z) => frame >= z.start && frame < z.start + z.duration);  (zoomAt repeats the same scan, so two O(zooms) scans per frame)

src/Composition.tsx:23-24 -- const frame = useCurrentFrame(); const camera = zoomCamera(zooms, frame);  (runs on every Remotion frame; the same render also runs clips.filter(...).map(...) with assets.find(...) per clip at :60-63 and :96-99)
src/export.ts:170 -- const zoom = screen ? zoomCamera(zooms, frame) : { scale: 1, x: 0, y: 0 };  (once per exported frame)

Measurement (throwaway /tmp Node 26 script, 222,749 samples spread over 10 min, 18,000 frames): samples.find(range predicate) 8,601 ms total, 0.478 ms/frame mean; samples.filter(300 ms window) 51,588 ms total, 2.866 ms/frame; binary search 15 ms total, 0.0008 ms/frame.
demoted.suggested_fix: Before the cursor work lands, put frame-to-sample lookup behind one pure function in timeline.ts shared by Composition.tsx and export.ts, backed by samples sorted by source time (ideally Float32Array/Float64Array columns rather than 222k objects) and a binary search, or a monotonic cursor index for the sequential export loop. Compute smoothing over an index range [lo, hi) from two binary searches instead of filter. While there, have zoomCamera find the active zoom once and pass it to the scale computation instead of calling zooms.find twice per frame. Add a unit test that evaluates 18,000 frames against a 200k-sample fixture under a time budget so a linear implementation fails.

triage_groups.title: One stage and source-time model for preview and export
triage_groups.context: The Remotion preview, the canvas exporter, the mark-mouse overlay and the export test each restate the 1280x720 stage, the mask table, the cover fit, the music gain and the timeline-to-source arithmetic.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Pin the preview transform first (#17) so the refactor has a net. Then land the React-free stage module (#1), extract drawFrame on top of it (#26), and add clipAt/sourceFrame (#22) and the shared gain constant (#32) in src/timeline.ts.
triage_groups.why: The trim-aware cursor and click-generated zooms need every one of these facts in JS on both renderers. One module turns a five-site edit into one and lets a unit test compare the preview and export projections.

triage_groups.title: Export speed and memory
triage_groups.context: Both are per-item allocations inside the export loops of src/export.ts: one audio node pair per decoded buffer, one full-size canvas per decoded frame.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Fix the audio mix first (#2): one source node per clip, verified with an export of at least 60 s of AAC or Opus audio. Then pass poolSize to CanvasSink (#25) and confirm with the existing HD and 4K export specs.
triage_groups.why: The audio mix is the one that makes exports longer than the demo sit at 0% for minutes; the canvas pool is a one-line change in the same function.

triage_groups.title: Saving, reopening and losing unsaved work
triage_groups.context: Three ways a session becomes unsaveable or is discarded (the string-size cap, an unreadable source file, a logo click that reloads), plus two traps in the project format code they share.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Ship the cheap guards first: the size precheck with an actionable message (#3, short-term step) and the beforeunload guard with a non-navigating logo (#23). Then decide the container change once (#3, structural step), because the read/write pairing in #29 and the per-asset pointer data ride on the same format work. Make the re-import remedy real (#28) and tighten the refusal test (#34) while in src/project.ts.
triage_groups.why: There is no autosave, so each of these ends in lost work. Owner decisions inside the queue: whether save embeds only referenced assets (#3) and relink-by-name versus snapshotting bytes at import (#28).

triage_groups.title: CI and test gates that pass when they should fail
triage_groups.context: The shrink-only baseline gate, the performance gate and the export pixel gate each accept the regression they are named for; browser journeys run on the dev server only; nothing runs before a change reaches main.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Apply the comparison-base change (#4) first; it is one line. Tighten the export pixel gate (#31) and the performance gate (#16) after reading their real baselines from CI logs. Add the production-bundle Playwright project (#18). Stop at #35: whether CI runs on pull requests is the owner's workflow decision, and it changes which base ref #4 passes for a PR.
triage_groups.why: These gates are what the next features will be merged against; each currently reports green for the failure it exists to catch. #35 is a decision item, not part of the apply queue.

triage_groups.title: Edit operations and undo history
triage_groups.context: Split, trim, delete and undo live in closures inside App.tsx and Timeline.tsx with no direct tests: IDs collide, no-op edits and slider ticks fill the history, and a trim commits a stale snapshot.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Fix the duplicate ID first (#13); it corrupts the edit and blocks Save. Then fix `change` once (#5): skip value-equal edits and coalesce continuous input, which also removes the undo symptom of #15. Add the Timeline guard for the playback pause (#15) and commit trims by clip id (#38). Cover the result with the journey in #20, or take its structural option (a pure reducer next to src/timeline.ts) first so the other four fixes are unit-testable.
triage_groups.why: One shared cause: edit-mutating logic is reachable only through the browser. The next features add more edit operations on the same state.

triage_groups.title: Keyboard, transport and mode state in App
triage_groups.context: The global keydown handler, the frame state versus frameRef split, and the markingMouse boolean each let the UI disagree with the real editor state.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Add the early modifier return (#7). Sync frame state on the Player's pause event and read frameRef in the transport buttons (#21) before touching rewind throttling (#36), because both edit the same frameupdate listener. Replace the markingMouse boolean with the zoom id it was armed for (#6).
triage_groups.why: Each is a small, local change in src/App.tsx, and three of the four are user-visible today.

triage_groups.title: Zoom model: placement rules, coordinate space and anchoring
triage_groups.context: Zoom invariants are enforced only in UI handlers, the shared ramp math has no ramp assertions, and two properties of a stored zoom (its focus unit and what it is anchored to) are undecided.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Mechanical first: add the ramp and pan assertions (#12), move the placement rules into src/timeline.ts (#8), then enforce them in parseProject with the same predicate (#10). Stop there. #24 (focus in source space or mask space) and #14 (zooms on absolute frames or anchored to source time) need the owner's decision; decide them together.
triage_groups.why: Both decisions define what a persisted zoom means, and click-generated zooms will write that format. Deciding after they ship means a project-file migration.

triage_groups.title: Import and startup failure handling
triage_groups.context: A failed file in a multi-file import is reported as success, and a stalled demo download keeps the editor inert with no way to import.
triage_groups.preferred_resolution: Collect import failures and report them with the count (#9); add a fetch deadline and Promise.allSettled with URL cleanup to loadDemo (#37).
triage_groups.why: Both hide a failure from the user at the point where they bring their own media in.
